title: 1.e4 Part 2: Sicilian
description: In Part 2 of the e4 course, the focus is on the Sicilian Defense. Levy's main recommendation is 2.a3, the Mengarini. Of course, we have many other weapons vs the Sicilian Defense here on Chessly as well.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2nb4/1N1qp3/3P4/2P5/5PPP.text:
Black tries to use the fact that the e-pawn has moved in order to defend c7 with the bishop.

We attack Black's queen with Bc4, another strong idea! 

The bishop on c4 is tactically defended since capturing it would lead to Nxd6+ with a fork of Black's king and queen.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2nb4/1N2p3/2BP4/2P5/5PqP.text:
Black doesn't fear death and grabs the pawn on g2.

We capture Black's undefended bishop with check.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2nb4/1N2p3/2BPq3/2P5/5PP.text:
Black moves the queen and gives a check on e4.

We block the check with the knight. 

Black now cannot capture the g2-pawn, since we would capture Black's undefended d6-bishop with check and follow it up with Rg1.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2nbp3/1N1q4/3P2Q1/2P5/5P.text:
Don't blindly rush with Bc4. There is a notable difference between ...e5 and ...e6. 

Instead, we play the crushing Qg4! 

We are threatening both the g7-pawn and Bc4 to trap Black's queen!

Black has no way to defend against both threats and White is completely winning.

r1b1k1nr/pp3ppp/2nbp3/1N1q4/3P4/2P5/5PPP.text: Black tries to use the fact that the e-pawn has moved in order to defend c7 with the bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp1np1pp/1q2Np2/1N1Pn3/5B2/2P5/.text:
We jump the knight into e6 with the aforementioned threats.

Black simply has no defense.

Our aggression on the e5-knight has provoked Black to make more weaknesses, which we exploited immediately.

r1b1kb1r/pp1np1pp/1q3p2/1N1Pn3/3N1B2/2P5.text: Black might also move their queen to b6.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3q4/3P4/N1P5/5PPP.text:
...Nf6 is very natural and happens 23% of the time, but it pretty much loses on the spot.

Black won't be ready for the aggression that's about to come.

We continue by jumping our knight into b5, threatening a fork on c7.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/2P5/5PPP/RN.text:
Black recaptures on d5 with the queen.

We continue by developing our knight to the edge of the board with Na3! 

From a3 our knight has access to the b5- and c4-squares, which will be crucial in all of the following lines.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3q4/3P4/N1P5/5PPP/.text:
...e6 is third in popularity and is equally as bad as ...Nf6 and ...e5.

You will face it 18% of the time.

We continue by jumping our knight into b5 and threatening a "family fork" on c7.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/3qp3/3P4/N1P5/5PPP/R.text:
The move ...e5 happens 26% of the time.

Black wants to challenge the center right away, also taking control of the f4-square.

We continue by jumping our knight into b5. This is our standard idea.

r1b3nr/pp1k1ppp/2nN4/4p3/2BP4/2P5/5PqP/R.text: Black moves the king and attacks our knight.

r1b3nr/pp1k1ppp/2nN4/4p3/2BP4/B1P5/5PqP/.text:
We defend the knight with Ba3 and are completely winning. 

If Black were to take our rook, we would crush their dreams with Qg4+. 

Otherwise, we can simply continue with Qf3 and be up a piece.

r1bq1bnr/p1N2ppp/p2k4/4p3/Q7/2P5/5PPP/2B.text: Black plays the only legal move and captures on d6.

r1bq1bnr/p1Nk1ppp/p2P4/4p3/8/2P5/5PPP/2B.text:
Black moves the king to d7 as to avoid giving up their queen.

Don't rush to capture the rook on a8! 

A much stronger response is Qa4+, which initiates a crushing attack on Black's king.

r1bqNbnr/p4ppp/p2k4/4p3/Q7/2P5/5PPP/2B1K.text:
We continue the attack with Ne8+.

Our bishops will quickly develop to a3 and c4 and Black's king won't be able to find any shelter. 

White is completely winning, the evaluation is astronomically high, and Black's best option is to give up their queen with ...Qxe8.

r1bqkb1r/pp1np1pp/5p2/1N1Pn3/5B2/2P2N2/5.text:
Black is desperate and defends the knight once more with ...f6.

But we jump our f3-knight into d4, taking advantage of the light-squared weakness on e6! 

Our threat is now Ne6, which intends to either fork Black with Nc7+ or to, in conjunction with Be3, trap Black's queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/8/1N1Pn3/5B2/2P5/5PPP/.text:
Black can't move the knight because that would give us access to the c7-square.

Instead, Black's only try is to defend the knight with ...Nfd7.

We attack the knight one more time with Nf3!

r1bqkb1r/pp2p1pp/1n3p2/1N1Pn3/3N1B2/2P5/.text:
...Nb6 is most common.

But it allows to remove one of the defenders now and go for another key idea.

We continue by capturing the e5-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp2p1pp/1n6/1N1Pp3/3N4/2P5/5PPP.text:
Black recaptures on e5.

We'll play the crushing Qh5+!

This is another move made possible by Black's ...f6 push.

r1bqkb1r/pp2p1pp/5p2/1NnPn3/3N1B2/2P5/5P.text:
...Nc5 is second most common but leads to the same thing as ...Nb6.

We continue by capturing the e5-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pp2p1pp/8/1NnPp3/3N4/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures on e5.

We play the crushing Qh5+! 

Black should probably resign, but can also play on and prolong their suffering.

r1bqkb1r/pp2p2p/1n4p1/1N1PQ3/3N4/2P5/5PP.text:
We capture on the pawn on e5. 

Black is simply dead lost as there is no way for them to defend against the combined threats of Qxa8 and Nc7+.

r1bqkb1r/pp2p2p/6p1/1NnPQ3/3N4/2P5/5PPP/.text:
We capture on the pawn on e5. 

Black can't defend against both threats and we are winning.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/1N6/3P4/2P5/5PPP/.text:
Black defends against Nc7 by retreating the queen to d8.

We continue the initiative by attacking Black's knight with d5! 

One of our main ideas is to develop the bishop to f4 in order to support Nc7+.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/1N1Pn3/8/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black moves the knight to e5.

We attack the knight again by developing our bishop to f4!

This gives us a tempo and forces Black to become even more passive.

r1bqkbnr/p4ppp/p2P4/1N2p3/8/2P5/5PPP/2BQ.text:
Black recaptures on a6.

We'll jump in with Nc7+!

This is a deadly combination.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PP.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6, and it's played over 40% of the time.

Black continues natural development and increases their control over the center.

We respond by offering up a pawn with b4!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP.text:
Most often, Black will continue by capturing the pawn on b4.

In particular, 73% of the time.

We'll recapture on b4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2P5/3P1PPP/R.text:
Black retreats the knight back to c6.

We establish a nice central structure by expanding with d4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1n2P3/8/2PP1PPP/RN.text:
Black challenges the authority of our gambit by capturing on b4 with the knight and has now officially won a pawn.

We'll attack Black's knight with c3 and force it to retreat. 

The move 5.c3 is also very beneficial since it will support a central expansion with d4.

r1bqkbnr/pp2nppp/3P4/1N2p3/8/2P5/5PPP/R1.text:
We continue with our plan by playing d6. 

White is completely winning.

The c7-square is now controlled by our pawn and Nc7+ is impossible to prevent.

r1bqkbnr/pp2nppp/8/1N1Pp3/8/2P5/5PPP/R1B.text: This is the other square Black's knight can retreat to, but it doesn't help matters whatsoever.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3PP3/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
You are, without question, going to face ...d5 almost half the time.

This move is probably most natural, but it also allows us to have the most fun.

We continue by capturing on d5.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1N6/3P4/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black defends against Nc7 by retreating the queen to d8. This is most common.

Don't rush with Bf4. Instead, we continue with d5! 

The main idea of this clearance sacrifice is to remove Black's pawn from the e-file, so that Bf4 can no longer be met with ...e5.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1N1p4/5B2/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
We develop our bishop to f4 and support the c7-square. 

Black doesn't really have a convenient way to prevent Nc7+ and White simply has a winning position.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1N2p3/3P4/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black defends against Nc7 by retreating the queen to d8.

We continue the initiative by attacking Black's knight with d5! 

SInce we can't play Bf4, our main idea is to march the pawn down to d6.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/n2P4/1N2p3/8/2P5/5PPP/R1.text:
Black desperately tries to hold on and defend c7 with ...Na6.

But we strike with Rxa6!, sacrificing the exchange and removing the defender of the c7-square.

A pretty logical tactic.

rbb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2n3q1/1N2p3/2BP4/1QP5/4N.text: Black retreats the queen to g6 and defends f7.

We simply castle our king. White now has a winning advantage. 

Black is horribly underdeveloped and we will combine the ideas of d5, Ba3, f4 and Ng3 in order to cause Black further headaches.

rbb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2n5/1N2p3/2BPq3/2P5/4NPP.text:
Black retreats the undefended bishop to b8, still covering the c7-square.

Since our bishop is already on c4, we can use this time to pressure another weakness.

So we develop the queen to b3 and attack the f7-pawn.

rbbnk1nr/pp3ppp/8/1N2p3/2BPq3/1QP5/4NPPP.text: Black can also defend f7 by giving up all hope and retreating their only developed minor piece to the back rank.

rbbnk1nr/pp3ppp/8/1N2p3/2BPq3/BQP5/4NPPP.text:
We continue with Ba3. 

White is completely winning. We will continue by castling our king and Black will struggle to get their king to safety.

Black's pieces simply look sad.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5. 

You will face this 18% of the time, and it was played in almost 660 million games!

The move ...c5 introduces asymmetry into the position, and its primary purpose is to control the important d4-square.

In this course, we're going to play a3 to prepare a gambit with b4.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/1N1Pp3/8/2P5/5PPP/R1BQ.text:
Black retreats the knight and sets up for the next game with ...Nb8.

We continue with our plan by playing d6, adjusting to Black's play.

Since they committed with ...e5, the d-pawn now has no adversaries in its path.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 1, we will learn the basics of the a3 Sicilian! 

In our e4 Vienna course, we learned about 1.e4 e5 positions. 

I now want to give you the a3 Sicilian weapon when you encounter 1.e4 c5.

1rbqkbnr/n3pppp/pN6/1p1P4/8/2P1B3/5PPP/R.text:
Black moves the rook and attacks our knight.

We'll capture the bishop on c8.

1rnqkbnr/4pppp/R7/1p1P4/8/2P1B3/5PPP/3QK.text:
We capture the a6-pawn.

The material is now equal, but White has a very pleasant advantage.

We can develop pretty flexibly and the general ideas include Bf4, Nf3 and Qb3.

1rnqkbnr/4pppp/p7/1p1P4/8/2P1B3/5PPP/R2Q.text: Black recaptures with the knight, and this is the only move which doesn't immediately lose.

1rq1kbnr/n3pppp/p7/1p1P4/8/1QP1B3/5PPP/R.text:
We simply defend the c-pawn with Qb3. 

We will follow up with by capturing Black's knight on a7 and the b5-pawn will fall due to an eventual Bxb5+. 

According to the engine, White has a +6 advantage in this position.

1rq1kbnr/n3pppp/p7/1p1P4/8/2P1B3/5PPP/R2.text:
This is natural but losing. 

Black recaptures with the queen, defending the a-pawn and counterattacking the c-pawn.

2r1kb1r/Rp2pppp/5n2/3q1b2/3P4/2P2N2/5PPP.text:
We can simply develop our knight to f3. 

The position is pretty pleasant and we will continue to develop with Qa4+, Be2 and O-O.

2r1kb1r/Rp2pppp/5n2/3q1b2/3P4/2P5/5PPP/2.text: Black can also continue by naturally developing with ...Nf6.

2r1kbnr/Rp3ppp/8/3q1b2/3Q4/2P2N2/5PPP/2B.text:
Magnus' move was okay, but we can still improve on his play with Qxd4. 

We want to trade queens and quickly develop with Bb5+ and castle.

White has a pretty pleasant position and a modest advantage.

2r1kbnr/Rp3ppp/8/3q1b2/3p4/2P2N2/5PPP/2B.text:
Black quickly releases the tension and captures on d4. 

This position occured between Carlsen and Inarkiev in 2017. 

The game was won by Magnus and continued Nxd4...

2r1kbnr/Rp3ppp/8/3qpb2/3P4/2P5/5PPP/2BQK.text:
Most direct is ...e5. 

Black expands in the center and immediately challenges our central structure.

We respond with Nf3, developing a piece and putting pressure on the e-pawn.

2r1kbnr/np2pppp/8/3q1b2/3P4/2P5/5PPP/R1B.text:
Black captures the knight on a7.

We recapture on a7.

2r1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1N1q1b2/3P4/2P5/5PPP.text:
Black defends c7 with the rook. 

This leaves the a-pawn hanging, but Black doesn't mind giving back the extra pawn in order to get some activity.

We capture the a7-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/q7/3P4/N1P2N2/5PP.text:
Black can also continue by developing with ...Nf6.

We develop our bishop to f4 and support the c7-square. 

We are now threatening Nb5, which would open up an attack on Black's queen and threaten a fork on c7 at the same time.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/q2n4/3P1B2/N1P2N2/5.text: Black jumps the knight into d5 and attacks our c-pawn and bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/q2n4/3P4/N1P2N2/3B1.text:
We respond by retreating the bishop back to d2. 

The c-pawn cannot be captured as after ...Nxc3 Qc1, Black loses a piece. 

We will continue to expand with c4 and follow it up with either c5 or d5.  

We'll develop the bishop to e2 and castle.

r1b1kbnr/1p2pppp/p1n5/3q4/3P4/N1P5/5PPP/.text:
Black responds with ...a6. This move controls the b5-square and it's played 14% of the time.

In a complicated sequence of moves, Nb5 isn't the best choice for White now.

We continue by jumping our knight into c4, threatening a fork on b6 instead.

r1b1kbnr/4pppp/p1P5/1p6/2N5/2P5/5PPP/R1B.text:
Black throws in an "intermezzo" and trades queens on d1, taking away our right to castle.

We play the only legal move and recapture on d1.

r1b1kbnr/4pppp/p1P5/8/2p5/2P2N2/5PPP/R1B.text:
We don't need to rush with Bxc4! 

We develop our knight to f3 first in order to prevent Black from expanding with ...e5. 

White has a comfortable advantage as we will be able to win the c4-pawn. Black's a-pawn will remain weak.

r1b1kbnr/4pppp/p1P5/8/2p5/2P5/5PPP/R1BK1.text: Black captures the knight on c4.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q4/3P4/2P5/5PPP/RN.text:
Black recaptures on d5 with the queen.

We continue by developing our knight to the edge of the board with Na3!

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/q7/3P4/N1P5/5PPP/R1.text:
This is the critical move! Black prevents our knight from moving and puts pressure on the c-pawn. 

...Qa5 is only played 1% of the time, but you need to know how to meet the critical response.

The sneaky Nf3 tactically defends the c-pawn, since ...Qxc3+ is met with Bd2, trapping Black's queen.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q7/3P4/N1P2N2/5PPP.text: Most common and objectively best is ...e6.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/qB6/3P4/N1P2N2/5PP.text:
We prepare to castle by developing the bishop to b5 and pinning Black's knight. 

The position is objectively equal.

If Black is slow to castle and "wastes" a move on ...Bd7, we can prepare a d5-break with c4.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1n2n2/8/2BP1B2/N1P2N2/.text:
Black plays ...a6 and prevents Nb5.

Another common idea is to push the d-pawn when we have the space and disorganize Black's pieces.

We attack Black's knight with d5. The pawn on d5 also serves as a guarantee that Black can't play ...e5.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/n2P4/2B2B2/N1P2N2/.text:
Black jumps the knight out to a5 and attacks our bishop, but we have a tactic ready.

We respond with the shocking Bb5+! 

The bishop cannot be captured since after ...axb5 Nxb5, Black has no good way of dealing with the threat of Nc7+.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/8/3P1B2/N1P2N2/5P.text:
Black steps off the a-file by retreating the queen to d8.

We continue by developing the light-squared bishop to c4. 

We are now threatening Nb5, followed by the unstoppable Nc7+.

The usual ideas.

r1bqkbnr/1p2pppp/p1n5/8/2NP4/2P5/5PPP/R1.text:
Black defends against Nb6 by retreating the queen to d8.

We continue the initiative by attacking Black's knight with d5!

As you can see, d5 is often a hidden and strong idea.

r1bqkbnr/4pppp/p1n5/1p1P4/2N5/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black tries to solve their problems tactically by counterattacking our knight with ...b5.

We'll take on c6.

r1bqkbnr/n3pppp/p7/1p1P4/2N5/2P1B3/5PPP/.text:
Black has to play energetically with ...b5. 

This move is important since it will allow Black to attack and remove our knight when it jumps into b6.

We continue by jumping our knight into b6 and attacking Black's rook and bishop anyway.

r1bqkbnr/np2pppp/p7/3P4/2N5/2P5/5PPP/R1B.text:
Black retreats the knight to a7.

We'll continue with Be3, supporting the b6-square for our knight.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PP.text:
The main continuation is 2...Nc6.

We respond by offering up a pawn with b4!

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP.text:
Most often, Black will continue by capturing the pawn on b4.

We recapture on b4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2n5/8/4P3/2P5/3P1PPP/R.text:
Black retreats the knight back to c6.

We establish a nice central structure by expanding with d4.

r1bqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/8/1n2P3/8/2PP1PPP/RN.text:
Black wins a pawn on b4.

We attack Black's knight with c3 and force it to retreat.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3PP3/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
You are, without question, going to face ...d5 the most. 

We continue by capturing on d5.

r2qkb1r/1p1bpppp/p4n2/nB1P4/5B2/N1P2N2/5.text:
Instead, Black blocks the check with the bishop and offers a trade.

We capture the bishop on d7.

r2qkbnr/1p1bp1pp/p4p2/3P4/2BN1B2/2P2Q2/5.text:
We simply continue by developing our light-squared bishop. White is already completely winning. 

We will castle our king and try to expose the horribly weak light squares in Black's position.

Black is underdeveloped and the Black king won't get castled anytime soon.

r2qkbnr/1p1bp1pp/p4p2/3P4/3N1B2/2P2Q2/5P.text: The bishop was attacked, so Black retreats it to d7.

r2qkbnr/1p2p1pp/p4p2/1N1Pnb2/5B2/2P2N2/5.text:
Black forces our knight to move by attacking it with ...a6.

We move the knight to d4 and attack Black's light-squared bishop.

r2qkbnr/1p2p1pp/p4p2/3P1b2/3N1B2/2P2n2/5.text:
Black can try to prevent the loss of material with Nxf3+.

We recapture on f3 with the queen.

r2qkbnr/pp2p1pp/5p2/1N1Pnb2/5B2/2P5/5PPP.text:
Black's only try is to defend the knight with ...f6.

We attack the knight one more time with Nf3! 

If our knight is now captured, we can simply recapture with the queen and Black's queenside will quickly collapse.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/1N3b2/3P4/2P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black can also defend against Nc7 by retreating the queen to d8. 

As we've seen in the previous study, this really isn't something Black should be doing.

We'll attack the knight with d5, also preparing Bf4 to support the c7-square.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/8/1N1Pnb2/8/2P5/5PPP/R1B.text:
Black moves the knight to e5.

We attack the knight again by developing our bishop to f4! 

If Black now moves the knight, we will simply win with Nc7+.

r3kb1r/1p1qpppp/p4n2/n2P4/2P2B2/N4N2/5PP.text:
We continue by supporting the d-pawn with c4. 

Our position is very pleasant and we will continue to improve it with O-O and Ne5.

Even with the most careful play, Black is still slightly worse.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n1q3/8/3P2b1/4NN2/3B1PPP.text:
We block the check with Ne3. 

Not only are we threatening to capture the b-pawn, but we are also threatening to win a piece with d5. 

Black doesn't really have a way to deal with both threats.

Notable is that we always want to be meeting ...Bxf3 with gxf3!

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n1q3/8/3P2b1/5N2/2NB1PPP.text: Black moves the queen to e6 and gives a check.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/3q1b2/3P4/N1P5/5PPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...Bf5 8% of the time.

Black develops the light-squared bishop and, consequently, frees up the c8-square.

We continue by jumping our knight into b5, threatening a "family fork" on c7.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/8/3P2b1/1q3N2/2NB1PPP.text:
Black moves the queen out of the attack.

We continue by attacking Black's queen once more with Rb1.

We will be targeting the b7-pawn as well.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/8/3P2b1/2q2N2/2N2PPP/.text:
Black "calls the bluff" and captures the c3-pawn with check.

We block the check and attack Black's queen with Bd2.

The idea is to grab as many tempi as we can and improve after giving up the pawn.

r3kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/q7/3P2b1/N1P2N2/5PPP/.text:
Nearly equally as popular as ...e6 is ...Bg4.

Black pins the knight and develops the bishop before playing ...e6.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2p5/1P2P3/P1N5/2.text:
Black chooses the fianchetto approach.

We will slide our rook to b1 prophylactically.

Also, we are planning to open up the b-file.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/1P2P3/2N5/2PP1.text:
Most often, Black looks to set up in "Dragon" style with ...g6 and ...Bg7.

We expand in the center with d4, naturally.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2p5/1P2P3/P7/2PP1.text:
Black develops their kingside knight and attacks the e-pawn 14% of the time.

We develop our queenside knight and defend it.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/8/1P2P3/8/2PP1PPP.text:
Black develops their kingside knight and attacks the e-pawn.

We develop our queenside knight and defend the attacked pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/1P2P3/2N5/2PP1PP.text:
Black can also look to develop with ...e6 and ...Be7.

Against 5...e6, we shouldn't rush with d4, since Black would be able to meet us with a quick ...d5.

Instead, we'll prioritize developing our kingside with Nf3, Be2 and castling.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

We will respond with a3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP.text:
Black plays ...d6 on move two 22% of the time, and it happened in more than 750,000 games.

Black's 2...d6 controls the e5- square, supports the c-pawn and activates their light-squared bishop.

Against this, we will play b4, looking to undermine Black's control of the d4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/3p4/8/1p2P3/P7/2PP1PPP/.text:
Black can also capture on b4, but this is inadvisable since Black relinquishes control over the important d4-square.

This happens almost half the time.

We'll respond by recapturing on b4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the ninth chapter! 

In this chapter, we will be concluding our analysis of the a3 Sicilian and taking a look at how to respond if Black chooses to play ...d6, ...d5, ...Nf6 or ...b6 on move two.

In this particular study, we will be taking a look at the flexible and non-confrontational 2...d6.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/2pq4/8/P4N2/1PPPBP.text:
We castle our king.

With a clear lead in development, White now simply has a better position.

Our plan is to expand in the center and on the queenside with c4, d4 and b4.

r1b1kbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2pq4/8/P4N2/1PPP1PP.text:
Black develops the queenside knight.

Let's develop with tempo on the queen now.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p4n2/1BpP4/8/P1N5/1PPP.text:
Expect to see ...a6 at some point.

We'll retreat to e2.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p4n2/2pn4/8/P1N2N2/1PPP.text:
Black captures on d5, restoring material balance.

Let's trade once.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/pn3n2/2pP4/8/P1N5/1PPPB.text:
Black jumps the knight into b6, opening up a triple attack on the weak d-pawn, which looks problematic.

We'll develop our knight to f3, though. 

We cannot hold onto the pawn, so we'll look to gain a significant lead in development while Black spends time winning it back.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/1BpP4/8/P7/1PPP1PP.text:
Black can also block the check with the b8-knight.

We'll develop our queenside knight and defend the d-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2p5/8/P1N2N2/1PPP1P.text:
Black goes back to d8.

We can continue in an aggressive fashion, this time activating the bishop to b5.

We are threatening to capture and disrupt Black's pawn structure.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4N3/P1P2N2/1.text:
We'll continue with c3, supporting the b4- and d4-squares. 

This was another idea behind Ne4.

White has a slight edge, and we'll look to continue with O-O and d4 or even b4.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2n1p3/1Bp5/4N3/P4N2/1PP.text: Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn.

r2qkbnr/pp1bpppp/2n5/1Bp5/8/P1N2N2/1PPP1.text:
That's why Black develops the bishop to d7 and supports the c6-knight.

How can we continue being aggressive?

We can jump to e4 and attack Black's c5-pawn now!

rn1qkb1r/pp1bpppp/5n2/1BpP4/8/P7/1PPP1PP.text:
Most often, Black blocks the check by developing the bishop to d7.

There is little merit to retreating here, so we'll trade.

rn2k2r/pp1qb1pp/4pn2/2p5/2P5/P4N2/1P1PQP.text:
We'll simply develop our knight to f3.

With an extra pawn and a clear target on e6, White is simply better and will have a relatively easy game. 

We can look to continue developing with O-O, d3 and Nc3.

rn2k2r/pp1qb1pp/4pn2/2p5/2P5/P7/1P1PQPPP.text:
Black recaptures with the pawn as to keep the queens on the board.

This is another reason behind Qe2; if Black doesn't want to trade queens down a pawn, they have to worsen their pawn structure!

rn2k2r/pp1qbppp/4pn2/2pP4/2P5/P7/1P1PQPP.text:
Black develops the bishop to e7, unpinning the pawn and preparing to castle kingside.

We have to capture on e6 at this point.

rn2kb1r/pp1q1ppp/4pn2/2pP4/2P5/P7/1P1P1P.text:
Black plays ...e6, looking to chip away at our pawn wedge.

That's why we will slide the queen to e2 and pin Black's e6-pawn.

The queen is now more active and participates in defending our pawn structure.

rn2kb1r/pp1qpppp/5n2/2pP4/8/P7/1PPP1PPP/.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

There are two attackers on the pawn now.

The only way to save it is c4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pq4/8/P4N2/1PPP1PP.text:
Black often develops the kingside knight, but this is inaccurate!

We can take the initiative by developing our knight to c3 and attacking Black's queen.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pq4/8/P7/1PPP1PPP/RN.text:
Black recaptures on d5 77% of the time.

This is now the Scandinavian Defense, but with the inclusion of a3 and c5.

We don't have to rush with Nc3 and can develop to f3 first.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/3P4/P1N2N2/1PP2.text:
We strike in the center with d4! 

White now has a pleasant, active position with easy development. 

We will look to develop with Be3, and in many cases Qe2 and O-O-O.

If Black captures on d4, we should recapture with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2p5/8/P1N2N2/1PPP1P.text: Black retreats the queen to its home square, d8.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pP4/8/P7/1PPP1PPP/.text:
Some players try to avoid losing the lead in development by attacking the pawn with 3...Nf6.

It occurs 20% of the time.

We will try to develop rapidly as well by giving a check on b5 with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c5.

Let's go for a3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP/.text:
Black chooses to strike in the center with ...d5.

This happens 4% of the time.

No reason not to capture and leave Black with a strong center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we will be taking a look at how to respond if Black chooses to meet our 2. a3 with the "Scandinavian-esque" 2...d5.

r1b1k2r/1pq1bppp/p1n1p3/2Pn2B1/4N3/P4N2/.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5, naturally.

We will trade the bishops on e7.

If Black recaptures with the queen, we can jump our knight into d6.

r1b1k2r/1pq1bppp/pnn1p3/6B1/2P1N3/P4N2/1.text:
Black retreats the bishop to e7.

The initiative doesn't stop! 

We attack the b6-knight with c5.

r1b1k2r/1pq2ppp/pnnbp3/6B1/2P5/P1N2N2/1P.text:
Black prevents Nb5 with ...a6.

But we'll attack Black's bishop by jumping our knight into e4 instead!

r1b1k2r/ppq2ppp/1nnbp3/6B1/2P5/P4N2/1P3P.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

We'll develop our knight to c3, threatening the deadly Nb5.

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p1n1/1N2q3/2P5/P4Q2/1.text:
Black jumps the knight into g6, defending against the threat.

We slide our queen to g3, forcing a queen trade. 

Black cannot decline the trade, since our queen and knight coordinate towards the c7-square!

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p1n1/1N6/2P5/P5q1/1P2.text:
Black trades queens on g3.

We recapture with the h-pawn. We are now threatening Nc7+.

r1b1kb1r/pp1pnppp/4p3/1N2q3/2P5/P4Q2/1P3.text:
Black moves the queen to e5 and gives a check to our king.

This is probably what you will face.

We block the check by moving our light-squared bishop to e2. 

We are now threatening the devastating Bf4.

r1b1kb1r/ppq2ppp/1nnpp3/4P1B1/2P5/P4N2/1.text:
So, Black moves the queen to c7.

Let's capture the pawn on d6 and finally relieve the tension.

r1b1kb1r/ppqp1ppp/2n1p3/3nP3/8/P4N2/1PP2.text:
Black moves the queen to c7 and adds an attacker to the e5-pawn.

We attack Black's knight with c4! 

The line that follows is pretty much completely forced.

If Black now retreats the knight to b6, we can simply continue with Bf4.

r1b1kb1r/ppqpnppp/2n1p3/4P3/2P5/P4N2/1P3.text:
Black retreats the knight to e7.

It's important to develop the knight to c3 and ignore the attack on the e-pawn.

You will see why.

r1b1kb1r/ppqpnppp/4p3/1N6/2P5/P4n2/1P3PP.text:
Black captures on f3 with check.

We'll recapture with the queen.

r1b1kb1r/ppqpnppp/4p3/4n3/2P5/P1N2N2/1P3.text:
Black captures the pawn on e5.

We can jump our knight into b5, attacking Black's queen.

r1b4r/1pq1kppp/p1n1p3/2Pn4/4N3/P4N2/1P2B.text:
We'll develop our bishop to e2, preparing to castle kingside. 

The c5-pawn is a thorn in Black's position, the d6-square is a potential outpost for our knight, and Black's king on e7 is misplaced. 

White is better.

r1b4r/1pq1kppp/p1n1p3/2Pn4/4N3/P4N2/1P3P.text: Black recaptures with the king instead.

r1bk1b1r/pp1p1ppp/4p1n1/1N6/2P5/P5P1/1P1.text:
We are down a pawn for the moment, but Black's position is simply dreadful. 

Not only are we likely to win the pawn back, but our pieces are also super active and we have a significant lead in development.

According to the engine, Black's only try is now ...b6, to which we will respond with Bf3 and Nxa7, winning our pawn back.

r1bk1b1r/pp1p1ppp/4p1n1/1N6/2P5/P5P1/1P2.text: Black defends c7 with the king.

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/3nP3/3Q4/P4N2/1P.text:
Black will attack our queen with ...Nc6 at some point.

We'll retreat the queen to its home square, d1.

From there it's safe and still has potential.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/1nnpp3/4P3/2P5/P4N2/1P3P.text:
Black retreats the knight to b6 instead.

We'll attack Black's queen with Bg5 now!

If Black now carelessly plays ...Be7, we can simply win a pawn after Bxe7 and exd6.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2npp3/3nP3/8/P4N2/1PP2PP.text:
By far the most common is ...d6, since Black is looking to get rid of our e-pawn.

But we won't play it slow and give Black what they want.

We start an initiative by attacking Black's knight with c4!

If Black now retreats the knight to c7, we can simply continue with Bf4.

r1bqkbnr/p2ppppp/1pn5/8/3QP3/P7/1PP2PPP/.text:
Black develops the knight to c6 and attacks our queen, which is expected.

We slide the queen back to d3.

Wasting this tempo is not the end of the world, since Black has committed to b7 with the bishop, which is a bad square.

r2qkb1r/pb1ppppp/1pn2n2/8/4P3/P1NQ1N2/1P.text:
We develop our other knight to f3. 

The dominant central presence and Black's misplaced light-squared bishop give White a pleasant edge.

We'll look to develop our dark-squared bishop next and castle queenside.

r2qkbnr/pb1ppppp/1pn5/8/4P3/P2Q4/1PP2PPP.text:
Black fianchettoes the light-squared bishop.

It's not all that active, though.

We'll simply develop our knight to c3.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4p3/3nP3/3Q4/P7/1PP2PP.text:
Black plays ...e6, defending the knight and opening up the f8- bishop.

We develop our knight to f3 in a standard manner.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e-pawn 2% of the time.

It's logical to push e5 and counterattack the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/2pnP3/8/P7/1PPP1PPP/.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5.

We'll strike in the center with d4!

We don't have to play b4 like usual here.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/8/3nP3/3p4/P7/1PP2PPP/.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

We recapture on d4 and attack Black's knight.

rnbqkbnr/p2ppppp/1p6/2p5/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP.text:
Black plays ...b6 only 1% of the time, preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and supporting the c5-pawn.

We don't really have to go b4 now. 

Instead, we'll quickly strike in the center with d4!

rnbqkbnr/p2ppppp/1p6/8/3pP3/P7/1PP2PPP/R.text:
Black captures on d4.

We'll recapture on d4 with our queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/8/2p5/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for 1...c5.

Let's go for a3.
